title: The World of AI: AI Courses catalogue with verified sources
answer: This is a catalogue page from The World of AI listing AI courses, 13 in total and 11 free, each with one verified source and a last verified date of 2026-09-27. The most useful thing it says is that the choice between university and industry courses is really about learning style: the four university graduate courses with public materials are described as exam driven theory, while the industry courses are code first and hands on. It does not report enrolment or completion figures.

sections.body: The World of AI publishes this page as part of its AI Research and Learning section, one entry in a wider site built from a single database covering state AI laws, a lawsuit tracker, a glossary, a tools directory, AI companies, a research library, an MCP server registry, compliance frameworks, sources, people, calculators and weekly digests. It is a catalogue of AI courses rather than an article or report. The page states it was last verified on 2026-09-27 and that source links are re-verified daily. Membership is described as editorial, based on significance rather than sponsorship, and the page says nothing on it is paid placement. It carries a suggested citation and a note that the site is free to read, free to cite and free to query.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The page is a curated catalogue of AI courses, organised by level and audience, each with one verified source, and listing duration, cost and what the course teaches. The entries named in the harvested text are DeepLearning.AI on Coursera at beginner level for managers and executives, DeepLearning.AI on Coursera at intermediate level for people who have finished the ML Specialization, Dataquest at beginner level for developers wanting hands on practice with LLM APIs on a subscription, fast.ai at beginner to intermediate level for programmers and top down learners, free with companion code, and a DeepLearning.AI and Stanford course on Coursera described as the first course for most people. A summary paragraph says all ten courses tracked offer free access to their core materials, though three pair that with a paid certificate option or public code repositories. Four are university graduate courses with public materials, Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285 and MIT's 6.S191, while the rest come from industry, DeepLearning.AI, Google, Hugging Face, fast.ai and Andrej Karpathy. The page says this split matters because university courses are generally structured around exam driven theory while the industry courses are described as code first or hands on, so the choice is about how someone wants to learn rather than which is more rigorous. Only three list a public code repository, fast.ai, Karpathy's Zero to Hero and MIT's 6.S191. The data does not report enrolment numbers, completion rates or which course is most widely taken.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source gives these numbers: 13 AI courses, 11 of them free, 3 with public companion code, curated by level and audience with one verified source each, re-verified daily, last verified 2026-09-27. Its body text instead says all ten courses tracked offer free access to core materials and that four are university graduate courses, so the page's own counts do not agree. Costs are listed per course: free to audit with a certificate fee, paid certificate, subscription, and free. Three courses are named as having public code repositories, fast.ai, Karpathy's Zero to Hero and MIT's 6.S191. The source states it does not report enrolment numbers, completion rates or which course is most widely taken.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in education can use this page as a catalogue of the courses and credentials the field currently uses, which is what the citing page claims for it. It shows the levels and audiences providers are targeting, from managers and executives to developers and graduate students, and it separates university graduate material from industry material on the grounds of teaching style rather than quality. It also maps the skills taught to the site's AI Skills Graph, which makes it a starting point for tracing what is taught rather than how well it works. Because it is re-verified daily, it is a live inventory rather than a fixed report.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Education

sections.body: The page is a directory entry, not a study. It gives no enrolment numbers, completion rates, learner outcomes or evidence about which course is best, and it says so. It does not date the courses themselves, explain how courses are selected beyond significance rather than sponsorship, or describe any evaluation method. The harvested text lists only five course entries while the header claims 13, so the catalogue appears partial here. The page sits on a site that also promotes books by Stephen R. Jordan, SRJ Consulting and Services, a novel titled The AI Lawyer, and a set of named audit products, so commercial material surrounds it even though the page states nothing on it is paid placement.
